about:
RL Hudson was founded in 1980 in Tulsa, Oklahoma, as a distributor of rubber O-rings to the regional oil industry. The company expanded nationally by 1985, added an in-house engineering department in 1991, and began manufacturing mandrel-formed hoses in 1996. Plastic injection molding capabilities were added in 1999, and operations relocated to Broken Arrow, Oklahoma, in 2004. Leadership includes Chairman Rick Hudson and CEO Jason Hudson.

The company specializes in custom plastic injection molding, rubber component manufacturing, and value-added unit assembly. Its plastic molding uses scientific (decoupled) injection molding on presses from 85 to 4,000 tons with real-time AuthenTIG monitoring. Rubber capabilities include injection, transfer, and compression molding, plus wrapped and extruded formed hoses. In-house tooling design, machining, and maintenance support production, while plastic welding covers ultrasonic, spin, hot-plate, and vibration methods. A 2024 expansion added a high-volume automated assembly line.

RL Hudson serves OEMs across automotive, HVAC, medium and heavy trucks, outdoor power equipment, powersports, agriculture, appliances, marine, power generation, waterworks, heavy equipment, material handling, and on-highway engine industries. Customers include material handling OEMs, outdoor power equipment manufacturers, and on-highway engine makers who rely on the firm for part consolidation, metal-to-plastic conversions, and complex multi-component assemblies.

The company emphasizes end-to-end solutions, combining design engineering, error-proofing, and rigorous quality control under one roof. Its integrated molding and assembly model aims to deliver faster turnaround, tighter quality control, and cost-effective part consolidation with a zero-defect mentality.

about:
Race Tech Race Cars and Components, Inc. operates from Burlington, North Carolina, where it has built custom race cars since 1988. The company was founded by Russ Farmer, a champion driver and builder who remains president and CEO. What began as a specialist in dragster construction has grown into a full-service race-car manufacturer serving competitors across multiple classes.

The shop produces complete dragsters, roadsters, and doorslammers, each designed in CAD and fabricated in-house. Capabilities include aluminum and sheet-metal fabrication, MIG/TIG welding, tube bending, and CNC plasma cutting on a 4-by-8-foot table that handles aluminum, steel, and stainless up to 1/4-inch thick. Race Tech also assembles AN braided-stainless hoses as an authorized Goodridge distributor and provides in-house powder coating, polishing, chroming, custom painting, and graphics. A parts division stocks accessories and hardware, including Grade 8 fasteners used throughout its builds.

Customers range from NHRA world champions and big-money bracket racers to local enthusiasts. Recent winners in Race Tech cars include Brian Weber at Famoso Raceway, TG Paschal at Piedmont, and Anthony Bertozzi at the NHRA Sportsman Nationals. The company also serves local racers with nitrous bottle refills and one-off fabrication projects such as fuel cells, carts, and structural components.

Farmer started the business to deliver race cars that combine reliability with ease of maintenance. Design features such as optimized driveline angles, 4-link brackets tuned for instant-center location, a removable crossmember for transmission access, and a master cylinder mounted outside the driver compartment reflect that focus. The in-house finishing suite eliminates outsourcing delays, giving teams a single source from chassis to paint.

about:
Radcliff Wire, Inc. is based in Bristol, Connecticut, a historic center of spring manufacturing in the eastern United States. The company began over six decades ago as a supplier of hard-to-find flat and shaped wire to spring makers, and word of its quality and reliability spread quickly.

Today Radcliff Wire produces flat, square, and custom-profiled wire in more than 60 metals and alloys. It manages the entire production chain in-house, from raw-material certification through drawing, shaping, and final inspection. The facility maintains a suite of testing equipment — including Rockwell and micro-hardness testers, tensile testers, laser micrometers, and optical comparators — to verify mechanical properties and dimensional accuracy on every order.

The company serves a diverse industrial base that includes aerospace, electronics, medical devices, automotive, and consumer-products manufacturers. Its wire goes into springs, contacts, surgical components, and other precision parts where consistent metallurgy and tight geometry are critical.

Radcliff Wire attributes its longevity to a quality system certified to ISO 9001:2015, a cross-trained workforce that averages 15 years of experience, and a compliance program that covers REACH, RoHS, conflict-minerals, and DFARS requirements. The firm was founded to fill a gap in the spring-wire market and continues to focus on delivering the exact wire specification a customer needs, when they need it.

It also runs a manufacturing complex capable of prototyping, low‑rate initial production, and hardware/software reverse engineering. The firm employs over 500 people across corporate facilities in nine states and project offices in fourteen states and one foreign country; intelligence work accounts for roughly 40 % of revenue.

Primary customers include the U.S. Army SMDC, the Intelligence Community, INSCOM, SOCCOM, NASA, and other DoD agencies. Testimonials cite the Chief of the Army’s High Energy Laser Division, the 116th MI Brigade Commander, and INSCOM’s G3 AISR Division Director as references.

The founders’ original goal – to prioritize the customer’s mission over profit, trust employee‑owners to do the “right thing,” and tackle problems others call impossible – still drives the culture. Employee ownership is cited as a differentiator that aligns workforce incentives with game‑changing solutions.

old_description: Since 1982 • Family Owned • Built to Perform • Rotomolded in the USA • Traffic Safety • Material Handling • Custom OEM Solutions • Serious Capacity • Real Relationships
about:
Remcon Plastics was founded in November 1982 by Peter and Doren Connors in Pennsylvania. The venture was backed by the savings of both families — Bill and Nancy Remmey (Doren’s parents) and Lorraine Connors (Pete’s mother) — and named Remcon in their honor. The founders bet that a small, family-owned rotational molding company could compete with larger manufacturers by building better products and standing behind them. In 1990, after eight years in Conshohocken, the company moved to Reading, Pennsylvania, tripling its plant size.

Today, Remcon operates a 75,000-square-foot facility in Reading with eight rotational molding machines. It produces material handling containers, MASH-compliant water-filled traffic barricades and longitudinal channelizers, and custom OEM rotationally molded components. Automation and advanced production systems enable output levels uncommon in rotational molding, supporting steady production and reliable deliveries. Key engineering innovations include the reinforced beaded 'R' lip that eliminated a common bulk-bin failure point, and a replaceable pallet system that extends container life by separating the wear component from the structural body.

Remcon serves traffic safety, material handling, and custom OEM markets. Its traffic safety line includes MASH-compliant water-filled barricades and channelizers built for real-world jobsite performance. Material handling products range from bulk bins and hoppers to the FBP bin with an integrated pallet. The company also provides custom rotational molding for OEM customers; one of its first OEM accounts from the early 1980s remains a customer today. Products are sold through a network of regional representatives across the United States and territories.

The company’s differentiation rests on durability, disciplined engineering, and integrity. Founder Pete Connors, an engineer with an MBA, applied stress-crack-resistant polyethylene formulations from DuPont to re-engineer common failure modes, raising industry standards for bin longevity from 12–24 months to over 10 years. Remcon remains family-owned and actively led by the founder, with the next generation — Tracy Connors as Executive Vice President and CEO, and James Connors as Director of Design — bringing outside experience to modernize operations while preserving the original commitment to keeping their word.

name: Resonant Link Medical: Wireless Technology for Next-Generation Implantables
old_description: Make power an asset, not a hurdle, to your medical device with the fastest and most patient-friendly wireless power and charging for bioelectronics.
about:
Resonant Link Medical is based in Burlington, Vermont, and was co-founded in 2017 by Aaron Stein, who serves as chief technology officer. Stein’s postdoctoral work at Dartmouth College on resonant coils and high-efficiency power electronics laid the technical foundation for the company’s wireless power platform. The venture was launched to eliminate the power and data bottlenecks that constrain next-generation implantable medical devices.

The company develops the Aurion WPT™ platform, a wireless power and data system that uses inductive transfer to recharge or continuously power implants through the skin without transcutaneous leads. Its product lineup includes Eterni™ for tiny implants (up to 500 mW continuous power for millimeter-scale devices), Vivigo™ Fast Charger (20-minute recharging over a large range), and Cardessa™ High Power Platform (10–15 W of driveline-free power for circulatory assist and other high-draw applications). Resonant Link also provides feasibility studies, regulatory-ready design integration, and traceable verification testing. To date, the platform has been used in the design of more than 50 implantable device types.

Customers span neuromodulation, cardiac rhythm management, sensing and diagnostics, circulatory assist, cranial and brain-computer interfaces, sleep apnea, implantable drug delivery, urinary and gastrointestinal, and smart orthopedics. Notable collaborations include work with Paradromics on a brain-computer interface system, Opto Biosystems on neurological disorder therapies, Lura Health on preventative care, and Resonetics on bioelectronic devices. In one case, the company helped a BCI developer reach human-study approval within 15 months of starting development.

Resonant Link positions its technology as the fastest and most patient-friendly wireless charging for bioelectronics, citing 10× faster charging over twice the range of conventional systems. The platform enables implants as small as 3 mm, maintains power transfer during patient movement, and supports deeper implantation sites. The firm emphasizes that its regulatory-ready processes and testing infrastructure reduce development risk and accelerate time to market for medical device manufacturers.

The Austin, Texas fab, acquired in 2025, brings 200 mm equipment, a 114,000 sq ft class 1 cleanroom, 30,000 sq ft of probe and test, and 65 nm+ capability.

The foundry serves fabless companies, integrated device manufacturers, OEMs, startups, government agencies, and research organizations across quantum computing, automotive, aerospace and defense, high-performance computing and AI, industrial, and biomedical markets. Its DMEA-accredited supplier status qualifies it for radiation-hardened and other mission-critical programs.

SkyWater differentiates itself through a collaborative Technology-as-a-Service model that aims to accelerate customers from concept to production, secure domestic supply chains, and support national technology leadership.

about:
Sloan Medical operates from Omaha, Nebraska, as a family-owned business founded by urologist Stewart Sloan. The company began over three decades ago when Sloan, drawing on firsthand experience in the operating room, set out to create protective gear that addressed the real challenges surgeons face during procedures.

The company manufactures two primary product lines. Sta-Dri includes impermeable knee-high coverings, aprons, bootleg leggings, and non-skid shoe covers that have passed ASTM F1671 viral penetration resistance testing. The ezGLIDE line consists of sterile, disposable single-use patient transfer sheets designed to replace reusable transfer boards and eliminate the cleaning products those boards require. All items are produced in North America using a one-size-fits-all approach that consolidates inventory to a single SKU per product, and most orders ship within 24 hours.

Sloan Medical serves hospitals, surgical centers, and veterinary facilities across the United States. Its PPE is used by surgeons, circulating nurses, OR technicians, and other frontline staff, while the ezGLIDE sheets support patient transfers in nursing facilities and postmortem care settings. The company also sells through a distributor network that includes American Medical Depot, Bowers Medical Supply, Healthmark Industries, and Medline Industries.

The business was built on the premise that PPE should be designed by clinicians who understand the operating room. That origin drives a focus on impermeability, comfort, non-skid safety, and durability—backed by ASTM testing and domestic production to avoid overseas supply disruptions. Personalized service remains a stated priority, with the company emphasizing direct access over layered sales structures.

old_description: From groundbreaking audio production consoles to innovative personal studios, Solid State Logic are the world's leading manufacturer of creative tools for music, live sound and broadcast.
about:
Solid State Logic was founded in 1969 by Colin Sanders CBE in the village of Stonesfield, Oxfordshire, United Kingdom. The company began by building switching systems for pipe organs before Sanders established Acorn Studios and produced the first SSL console, the A Series, in 1976. The business moved its headquarters to Begbroke Manor in 1986, adding a 4,000 m² manufacturing facility that opened in 1988 and remains the UK headquarters today. A U.S. office is maintained in New York, New York.

The company designs and manufactures analogue and digital audio consoles, audio interfaces, DAW controllers, analogue outboard processors, and software plug‑ins for music production, live sound, and broadcast. Key product lines include the System T broadcast platform (S500, S400, S300), the L‑Series live sound consoles (L650, L550 Plus, L450), the Odyssey and Oracle studio consoles, the ORIGIN series, and the SSL 12/18 audio interfaces. Production occurs at the Begbroke Manor facility; headcount and annual volumes are not publicly disclosed.

SSL serves music recording studios, live sound engineers, broadcast facilities, post‑production houses, educational institutions, and installed‑sound venues. Notable installations include Spiritland’s live mix facility in London, Shoreline College’s teaching studio in Seattle, and DVLP Academy’s training center. The company also supports OB and sports production, podcast and webcast workflows, and cloud‑based virtualised production.

SSL’s differentiation stems from a history of console innovation: the SL 4000 E Series (1979) introduced motorised fader automation (Ultimation) and the SuperAnalogue™ signal path; the 2000s brought hybrid consoles (AWS, Duality) that merged analogue summing with DAW control; and the System T platform pioneered native ST 2110 IP audio routing with automated NMOS discovery. The Odyssey console adds full analogue processing with console‑wide Instant Recall.

South Fork Industries operates in Maiden, North Carolina, where it began production in 1988 as a commission dyeing and finishing operation. The company has run continuously for over three decades, building a reputation for quality work and integrity in the textile processing sector.

The facility houses 14 dye machines, including pressure jets and soft-flow units, with load capacities ranging from 150 to 1,700 pounds. A centralized computer system controls the dye machines and links to an automated dye and chemical mixing room for precise adjustments. Finishing capabilities cover both tubular and open-width formats: two shrinkage-control belt dryers, 24 tumble dryers, four Fabcon compactors, and tubular napping for tubular goods; a Krantz eight-bay tenter frame with a 74-inch maximum width, a Fabcon open-width compactor, open-width napping, and tip shearing for open-width fabrics.

South Fork serves textile mills, apparel brands, and fabric converters that require commission dyeing and finishing, though the company does not publicly list specific customers or industry verticals beyond the general textile market.

The company differentiates itself through an on-site laboratory that specializes in color matching using Datacolor Color Management Solutions, and it conducts a full suite of physical tests—shrinkage, width, yield, stretch and recovery, torque, crocking, wash fastness, burst, and wicking—all performed to AATCC test methods.
